Apologies if this has already been answered or described in depth; there's a lot of text on regenesis and I haven't read all of it. So regenesis has tx witness + block witness. I'm wondering about tx sealing. Basically, which of these statements are (the most) correct?

1. Transactions are signed without witness. Witnesses are an appendage to a tx, and do not actually remain when the tx is inside a block body. 
2. Transactions are signed _with_ witness data, so all tx witnesses are also part of the block body

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content:
Is there a reason it cannot be this <@!211091239112671234>?
3. Transactions are signed without witness.  Witnesses are part of the block body.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Hmm, actually since the transaction signer has to pay for witness data, it *has* to be signed.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Otherwise a malicious miner could swap out an optimized witness for a worst-case-scenario witness payload and charge the transaction signer for it.

excerpts.author: sky.cactus
excerpts.content: Note: This assumes EIP-2711 doesn't get implemented first, which would allow for the sponsor to pay for witness inclusion (in fact, I would argue that is where witness data should live).

excerpts.author: .vbuterin

excerpts.content: If so, then verifying a transaction at network layer would be a not-that-easy task, and would fall under DoS risk...

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Now if on the other hand, we add a rule that says that if a tx call something not in the active state and not in the access list, that call fails but the execution continues

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: (which seems to be the only way to solve this conundrum)

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Then you get the problem that you would need a witness going down to that account to prove that the tx actually has that effect

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Unless you change the tree structure so that every node in the tree has a "last block modified" parameter

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Otherwise, how would a newly fast synced client know that the account is not recent

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Unless the idea is that fast syncing is only possible at all at epoch boundaries

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: But would be horrible, it basically introduces an "implicit state" that's not actually part of the merkle tree (namely, which accounts are active and which are not), which breaks a core invariant we've stringently maintained since day 1, and moves further away from the goal of full stateless verification being _possible_ (even if most clients don't do it)

Sorry, so, to re-express the above and summarize: consider the case where a transcation does a lot of execution and then unexpectedly calls into some account A, which may be active state and may be inactive state. The transaction does NOT include an explicit witness for A or have it as part of an access list.

Case 1: if A is inactive, transaction execution fails and the tx is invalid. This creates a DoS vuln.
Case 2: if A is inactive, the call fails but tx execution continues. This means that the fact of (whether or not there exists an active account at any address) must be part of the active state, which means one of three things:

(2.1) miners still need to download the full state tree, including active and inactive
(2.2) every node of the state tree, including intermediate nodes, have a flag that says "do I have at least one active child"
(2.3) the information of which accounts are active does not get merklized

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: I guess there's (2.4): there's a *separate* Merkle tree that keeps track of the set of active accounts?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content:
so imagine that I tell you I have a transaction T, which has  no witness and no access list and runs this code:
```
for i in range(1000000): x = (x * x * x + block.number + i)
z = extcodesize(CONST_ACCOUNT_ADDRESS)
sstore(x + z)
```
Where `CONST_ACCOUNT_ADDRESS` is an address that I do not yet tell you. If you "have the state", you must be able to fully execute T no matter what `CONST_ACCOUNT_ADDRESS` is. But the result of T depends on whether or not `CONST_ACCOUNT_ADDRESS` is active, because if it is inactive, then correct execution of T reverts, and if it is active, it saves some value in storage. Hence, the information of the whether or not any given account is active must be in the state.
But if this is true, we cannot leave the Merkle tree format unchanged, because (i) the Merkle tree currently does not say which accounts are active, but even more scarily (ii) if you are provided a subtree that does NOT include some range X...Y, then you have no way to tell whether or not there is some active account hidden inside X...Y. So this means you can't actually authenticate whether or not you received a correct state.

2. Smaller gas limits tend to be included earlier in blocks, as they are easier to fit in

excerpts.content: Nevertheless, ignoring the statistics, I feel confident in saying that being accurate at predicting gas costs is hard, especially when you have complex systems like DeFi where many contracts or states are touched by many independent users. People use higher gas limits than necessary because accurate estimations often lead to failed txs and I think this will be the same for tx witnesses

excerpts.author: sky.cactus

excerpts.author: sky.cactus

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Basically, the key benefit of bounding the witness size and enabling fully stateless verification is that an arbitrary subset of blocks can be verified. One concrete benefit in an eth2 context is that eth2 clients would only have to validate eth1 blocks (which is a very expensive procedure) when they happen to have been selected for that committee (ie. 1/2048 of the time) instead of always

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Also if we want to expand to multiple computation shards this becomes even more important

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Otherwise, one challenge with partial statelessness strategies is that if you do the math, it turns out that "active state" can grow in size pretty quickly

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: Here's one way to look at it: suppose we use current gas costs with no change. Then, the active state can grow by 400MB per block (this is the same calculation as that used to compute the witness size), so theoretically an attacker could generate a sequence of 25 blocks that would immediately make the active state larger than lots of people's RAM

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: so it's quite hard for partial statelessness to actually *guarantee* active-state-in-RAM, unless you... implement my proposed reforms that make accessing all state significantly more expensive

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: eg. if we set gas prices so the max witness size is 4 MB (my proposal 1 year ago), then you'd need at least half a day to get to that 10 GB (though maybe less if you include merkle branches), which is.... somewhat acceptable?

excerpts.author: .vbuterin
excerpts.content: so the easiest way to enable *both* stateless verification and partial statelessness a la regenesis without horrible tradeoffs is to adjust gas costs to clamp down hard on the max witness size of a single block, with 4 MB being my proposed limit that would come from SLOAD and EXT opcodes costing ~2500
